comparator.name: Dutch Languages and Cultures — Dutch Language and Culture route
comparator.sourceNotes: The current generic bachelor is Dutch Languages and Cultures (ISAT 50479). Its 2026–27 programme-specific Teaching and Examination Regulations define two formal tracks, Dutch Language and Culture and Frisian Language and Culture. Neither language-specific track is inherently broader or less specialized than the other, so the Dutch Language and Culture track is selected by the neutral official-order tie-break; it is listed first in the regulation. This choice is made before and independently of UCR fit. For students beginning in September 2026, the selected track has a coherent 60+60+60=180 EC curriculum. The second- and third-year parts take effect in 2027–28 and 2028–29 as this cohort progresses. The 30-EC minor remains genuine open curricular space and is not populated with an invented subject. The live programme page and the 2026–2027 regulations were rechecked on 2026-10-14; the settled neutral Dutch-route selection and 180-EC reconstruction remain unchanged.

comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The generic target covers a current bachelor with two equally formal, language-specific tracks: Dutch Language and Culture and Frisian Language and Culture. Current official evidence does not establish either as more representative, broader or less specialized. The Dutch Language and Culture track is therefore selected because it is listed first in the current official regulation, applying the neutral official-order tie-break before any UCR fit assessment.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest related-fields response integrates literature, rhetoric, language processing, public communication, media and research. Two further generator-backed directions are coherent and feasible: language, identity and multilingual societies, and literature, culture and heritage. The closest and multilingual routes differ by five courses (37.5 EC), the closest and literature routes by six (45 EC), and the two focused routes by ten (75 EC). All three preserve the absence of Frisian study and full Dutch or Frisian linguistics, proficiency and period-specific literature sequences.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Introduction to Literary Studies directly develops close reading and interpretation across literary genres, but not specifically in Dutch.
Great Literary Works gives chronological literary interpretation that includes medieval texts; it does not reproduce medieval Dutch literature.
Life & Travel Writing develops historical and cultural literary analysis, but not a dedicated early-modern Dutch sequence.
Film & Text provides advanced narrative, adaptation and textual analysis related to modern literary study, without Dutch-period specialization.
Perspectives on Literary Meaning combines theoretical approaches with a research project and is the strongest scheduled counterpart to literary research approaches.
Introduction to Brain & Behavior supplies cognitive foundations for text and language processing.
The Art of Rhetorical Communication directly studies rhetoric, argument and audience, without the comparator’s Dutch-language stylistics depth.
Style & Meaning analyses linguistic choices and meaning in texts; it is general stylistics rather than Dutch semantics.
Dutch develops introductory oral and written Dutch communication; it does not equal advanced academic language-proficiency development.
Persuasive Communication directly studies persuasion, framing and argumentation.
Creative Communication Laboratory studies and practises creative meaning-making through language and media, while not being Dutch creative-writing training.
Psycholinguistics directly studies language acquisition, processing and experimental methods, but not Dutch-specific acquisition.
Research Methods & Statistics supplies research design and quantitative foundations related to the programme’s research workshops.

notes.text: Groningen’s generic degree contains formal Dutch and Frisian routes; the neutrally selected Dutch route provides a disciplinary sequence in Dutch phonology, syntax, semantics, language change and proficiency, Dutch literature across historical periods, research workshops and a Dutch Studies thesis. UCR can build coherent related programmes through literature, rhetoric, communication, media, psycholinguistics, history, sociology and digital methods, including one introductory Dutch-language course, but it offers neither Frisian study nor a full Neerlandistiek curriculum.

UCR lacks the comparator’s cumulative Dutch phonology and syntax, historical Dutch, advanced Dutch-language proficiency, period-specific Dutch literature and compulsory Dutch Studies thesis. It also cannot supply the generic target’s Frisian proficiency, Old Frisian, Frisian linguistics and regional-history formation. Its adjacent analytical and research strengths must be read with those specialist gaps visible.
